title: RIPLRT Institute Research Group Manual
text:
Welcome to the RIPLRT Institute’s Research Group Manual
This is the operating system of the RIPLRT Institute — a mentee-powered environmental health, immunology, and respiratory health equity research group. We translate environmental exposures into equitable respiratory and immune health through exposure science, biochemical, microbiology, and immune biomarker discovery, computational approaches, reproducible analytics, bilingual science communication, and inclusive mentoring.
The RIPLRT Institute operates under Felix E. Rivera-Mariani PhD LLC. It is an independent research and mentoring organization and is not an entity, department, or administrative unit within organizations with which Dr. Félix E. Rivera-Mariani (founder, principal investigator and mentor) is affiliated with (Lynn University, the University of Puerto Rico). What the Institute does do is mentor and integrate students and early-career scientists from Lynn University and from outside Lynn University - at different stages of their careers - into its projects, its culture, and its workforce-development mission.
If you are reading this because you recently joined us: welcome. This manual is the fastest way to understand who we are, how we work, what we expect of one another, and how we give credit. If you are a returning member, treat it as a living reference — return to it when you onboard a new teammate, start a project, plan a manuscript, or hit a question about process. Note that this manual is not a static document. It is a living, evolving resource that we update as we learn and grow together. We encourage you to contribute to it by sharing your insights,suggestions, and feedback.
If you are joining through Lynn University, your work is carried out under the Educational Biomarker Discovery Lab (EBDL) — the umbrella through which RIPLRT-affiliated research operates within Lynn University. In short: the RIPLRT Institute (under Felix E. Rivera-Mariani, PhD, LLC) is the research group and its operating system; the EBDL is the Lynn University–housed branch through which Lynn-affiliated members conduct that work, subject to Lynn University policy. Members who join from other institutions, or independently, are mentored directly under the RIPLRT Institute.

We are a serious research organization and a humane mentoring environment. Those are not in tension. We use “we” language because the lab belongs to all of us — it is our research group, not only the PI’s. We state expectations directly because clarity is a form of respect. And we assume good faith, because that is how trust is built and how science gets done.

title: 2  Welcome to RIPLRT Institute
text:
2.1 What RIPLRT is
Welcome to the Respiratory and Immunology Project and Laboratory Research Team — the RIPLRT Institute. Whether you are a returning member or this is your first day, we are glad you are here.
This chapter orients you to what kind of place this is, what you can expect from us, and what we will ask of you in return.
The RIPLRT Institute, often referred to simply as the RIPLRT, is a research group, a learning environment, and a scientific home. We are a mentee-powered group studying how environmental exposures shape respiratory and immune health — and how to convert that understanding into tools that protect people, especially in communities that carry the heaviest environmental burden.
You joined because of the science, and our values and principles. We hope you stay because you feel valued, connected, mentored, and part of work that matters. Belonging is not a perk here; it is part of how we do good science. People who feel safe ask better questions, surface mistakes earlier, and take the creative risks that move projects forward.
While you are with us, you will develop skills across several domains:

This manual is the 2026 Edition (v2.0). It is the direct descendant of the 2018 RIPLRT Lab Manual and its 2021 revision, which were inspired by the open lab-manual movement and built reproducibly in R and Quarto. We have preserved the parts that made the original strong — the welcoming tone, our values, our commitment to integrity, open science, reproducibility, and clear authorship — and modernized everything else for who we are now: a hybrid computational and translational research and mentoring group operating across the RIPLRT Institute and affiliated entities.

title: 3  History and Evolution of RIPLRT
text:
3.1 Origins (2018–2021): the wet-lab phase
Knowing where we came from helps you understand why we work the way we do. The RIPLRT has evolved through distinct phases, and the current RIPLRT Institute is the most recent expression of a consistent through-line.
RIPLRT began as the Respiratory and Immunology Project and Laboratory Research Team within a College of Biomedical Sciences setting. The early group was organized around wet-lab immunology: human-based immuno-physiological approaches, molecular biology, and the immune effects of airborne pollutants crossing the respiratory barrier in susceptible people — those with asthma, respiratory allergies, and other chronic respiratory conditions. The group was small, focused on a few projects, and centered around the PI’s bench work. The mission was to understand how environmental exposures shape respiratory and immune health, with a focus on Puerto Rico’s unique environmental and health context. An example of this work can be found here.

We acknowledge the past members who built that foundation — it is the backbone of this manual.

3.2 Transition (2021–2024): from bench to hybrid
Over this period the group’s center of gravity shifted from the bench toward a hybrid computational and translational model. Several forces drove this:

The rise of large, biomarker-rich public repositories and surveillance datasets.
Biomarker discovery and interpretation as a key to understanding exposure-health links.
The need to translate insights into population-level forecasting and decision-support tools.
Maturation of reproducible analytics and AI/ML methods.
A strategic decision to scale impact through population-level forecasting and repository-based discovery alongside molecular work.
A broadening geographic frame to Puerto Rico, the Caribbean basin, and the southern coastal United States.

title: 4  Scientific Identity and Strategic Through-Line
text:
4.2 The strategic through-line
Our portfolio is large, but it is not scattered. Every project sits somewhere on a single chain:

Exposure Science — We measure and interpret environmental signals: bioaerosols and fungal spores, airway microbiome/mycobiome signatures, \(PM_{2.5}\), \(NO_2\), chemical and physical pollutants, meteorology, and wearable exposure streams.
Immune and Biochemical Bioactivity — We connect those exposures to immune and inflammatory biomarkers and to biological and biochemical responses and pathways.
Computational Modeling — We use AI/ML, distributed lag models, mixed-effects models, and equity-aware metrics to forecast exposure-linked respiratory risk windows. We also use computational methods to discover and interpret biomarker signatures of exposure and risk, and bioinformatic methods to link those signatures to biological pathways and potential therapeutic targets.
Equity-Focused Translation — We convert forecasts into clinician-facing dashboards, community risk briefs, public-health playbooks, and peer-reviewed science.
Inclusive Workforce Development — Across all of the above, mentees are embedded as active contributors, building an inclusive workforce in immunology, exposure science, environmental and respiratory health, computational biology, and data science.

When you describe your project, locate it on this chain. It clarifies your aims, your collaborators, and your authorship plan.

4.4 Where the science lives: data and methods
Our near-term implementation cycle emphasizes real-world and computational validation using existing surveillance, healthcare data, and biomarker-rich repositories rather than only new ex vivo functional assays. Core resources include:

Surveillance & claims: Puerto Rico fungal-spore and respiratory-virus surveillance; incoming PR Department of Health / ASES claims and pharmacy data.
National repositories: BioLINCC, BioData Catalyst, All of Us, MESA, Framingham, AsthmaNet, and NHANES.
Methods: AI/ML, distributed lag models, mixed-effects models, GWAS and polygenic risk scores, SHAP explainability, causal mediation analysis, multi-agent AI architectures, and equity-aware performance metrics (among others) — all within a reproducibility and equity-stratified analysis framework.







ImportantIdentity discipline



We frame new work as a forward progression, not a repetition of past work. Every proposal, talk, or project should be positioned as the next step on the through-line. This is both a scientific and a strategic habit — it keeps the program coherent and the narrative under our control.

title: 4  Scientific Identity and Strategic Through-Line
section: 4.5 Why equity is structural, not symbolic
text:
4.5 Why equity is structural, not symbolic
The communities we study — in Puerto Rico, the Caribbean, and coastal regions — face converging extreme weather, bioaerosol, pollution, and respiratory-health challenges and are often under-resourced and underrepresented in research. Equity is therefore built into the science itself: we stratify analyses by community, age, sex, and other relevant axes; we report equity-stratified performance; and we translate findings into bilingual materials communities can actually use. Equity is a design requirement of our pipelines, not a line in a diversity statement.

title: 5  Vision, Mission, and Core Values
text:
5.1 Vision
This chapter states what we are working toward, how we pursue it, and the values that govern how we treat each other and the science. It is adapted directly from Dr. Rivera-Mariani’s current Individual Academic Plan (IAP) so that the manual, the strategic roadmap, grant narratives, and recruitment all tell one coherent story.
Over the next five years, the RIPLRT Institute will advance a nationally recognized, equity-centered program in environmental immunology, exposure science, and computational respiratory and cardiovascular health.
Communities across Puerto Rico, the Caribbean basin, and the southern coastal United States face converging extreme weather, bioaerosol, pollution, and respiratory-health challenges that require predictive and preventive solutions. We will identify critical short- and long-term risk windows for respiratory exacerbations and exposure-related immune and cardiopulmonary outcomes by integrating biological exposures (airway microbiome/mycobiome signatures and bioaerosols) with non-biological exposures (\(PM_{2.5}\), \(NO_2\), chemical and physical pollutants, meteorology), immune and inflammatory biomarkers, wearable exposure assessments, and advanced computational modeling.
This vision is propelled by mentee-integrated research, bilingual science communication, and community-responsive translation that prevent disease, strengthen climate-health resilience, and narrow respiratory health disparities in environmentally threatened and socially underserved populations.
crumbs: 5  Vision, Mission, and Core Values

title: 5  Vision, Mission, and Core Values
text:
5.2 Mission
We conduct collaborative, extramurally supported, multi-cohort, repository-based, and prospective studies that temporally align bioaerosols, airway microbiota/mycobiota, chemical and physical pollutants, wearable and environmental exposure streams, immune and inflammatory biomarkers, respiratory symptoms, lung function, clinical severity, pharmacy utilization, and care pathways.
We leverage surveillance data, incoming healthcare data, and accessible national resources (e.g., BioLINCC, BioData Catalyst, ImmProt, NHANES, All of Us) to build reproducible analytic pipelines. Using computational approaches and AI/ML, we forecast exposure-linked risk windows and validate forecasts against real-world clinical outcomes.
Findings are translated into clinician-facing dashboards, community risk briefs, public-health playbooks, peer-reviewed manuscripts, and student-centered training products. Across every phase — from question generation and data access to analysis, authorship, presentations, and dissemination — mentees are embedded as active contributors to build an inclusive workforce.

title: 5  Vision, Mission, and Core Values
text:
5.3 Core Values
Our values are not decoration. They must be visible in daily behaviors and documented practices — what we reward, how we run meetings, how we resolve conflict, and how we assign credit.

5.3.1 Values preserved from our founding

Inclusiveness — everyone’s voice counts.
Multidisciplinary focus — we integrate disciplines rather than defend silos.
Diversity — we value and respect differences in perspective and opinion.
Integrity — we follow strict institutional, scientific, and ethical guidelines.
Productivity — we bring our best effort toward our goals, sustainably.
Innovation — we stay open-minded and learn from both successes and failures.
Excellence — we target the highest quality of scientific work.
Collaboration — what is done in isolation is usually done better in partnership.
Leadership — we cultivate intra- and inter-motivation and inspiration.



5.3.2 Values we add for the 2026 program

Psychological safety — people can ask naive questions, surface mistakes, and disagree with the PI without fear (?sec-psych-safety).
Reproducibility — if it isn’t reproducible, it isn’t finished.
Transparency — work lives in shared, version-controlled spaces; “no surprises” is the default in both science and communication.
Health equity — equity is a design requirement of our science, not an afterthought.
Community responsiveness — the communities we study are partners, not subjects.
Bilingual science communication — our science speaks Spanish and English, to specialists and to neighbors.
Responsible AI — we use AI to accelerate good work, never to outsource judgment or integrity (?sec-responsible-ai).







TipThe vision sentence you can quote anywhere




Our research group is dedicated to translating environmental exposures into equitable respiratory and immune health, and we make it happen by building reproducible, mentee-powered, community-responsive science.

title: 6  What It Means to Belong to RIPLRT
text:
6.1 Belonging is a retention strategy
People join The RIPLRT because of the science, and our values and principles. They stay because they feel valued, connected, and part of something larger than any single task. This chapter is about belonging — and why we treat it as a research strategy, not a nicety.
A research group is not only a productivity engine; it is a scientific home. Members who feel they belong stay longer, contribute more, ask better questions, and surface problems earlier. The lab should feel like our laboratory, not the PI’s laboratory with helpers attached.
This is a deliberate design choice. Connected teams can work fewer hours and still be more productive, because trust reduces friction: people coordinate faster, hide less, and recover from setbacks together.

title: 6  What It Means to Belong to RIPLRT
section: 6.2 The compact: what belonging gives and asks
text:
6.2 The compact: what belonging gives and asks
Belonging here is reciprocal.
What belonging gives you:

Membership in a shared mission, not a transactional “do this analysis and publish” relationship.
A name, a profile, and a voice in the group — your ideas shape projects.
Mentorship aimed at your trajectory, not only the project’s deliverables.
Visible credit for your contributions.
Rituals, traditions, and small celebrations that mark progress and make the work human.

What belonging asks of you:

Show up — to meetings, to deadlines, to each other.
Contribute to the climate: be the teammate who makes it safe for others to learn in public.
Bring problems early; “no surprises” protects everyone.
Help newer members the way more senior members helped you.
crumbs: 6  What It Means to Belong to RIPLRT

title: 6  What It Means to Belong to RIPLRT
text:
6.3 We design culture on purpose
Culture always develops — the only question is whether it develops by design or by accident. Left alone, culture tends to organize around urgency, the loudest personality, hierarchy, or stress. We choose instead to shape it around our values.
Concretely, that means:

Structure creates safety. This manual, project operating charters, clear ground rules, and explicit communication channels exist so that no one has to guess what is expected. Ambiguity is a tax on belonging; we minimize it.
Connection doesn’t require formality. Belonging is built in coffee chats, shared digital spaces, a monthly huddle, celebrating small wins, and showing up for one another — not only in formal meetings.
Rituals reinforce identity. Traditions like a recurring “RIPLRT Wins & Roadblocks” huddle help members working on different datasets feel part of one group.
crumbs: 6  What It Means to Belong to RIPLRT

title: 6  What It Means to Belong to RIPLRT
section: 6.4 Belonging across a hybrid, distributed group
text:
6.4 Belonging across a hybrid, distributed group
Many of us work remotely or across institutions and time zones. Belonging cannot depend on a shared physical room. We sustain it intentionally through:

A single primary messaging channel for quick, human, day-to-day connection.
Cameras-on-when-able norms for huddles, balanced against bandwidth and accessibility.
Asynchronous wins-sharing so contributions are seen even when schedules don’t overlap.
Deliberate inclusion of remote members in decisions, authorship, and visibility.
crumbs: 6  What It Means to Belong to RIPLRT

title: 6  What It Means to Belong to RIPLRT
text:
6.5 Measuring belonging
We treat belonging as something we can observe and improve, not just hope for. We run a brief anonymous quarterly pulse check (10 minutes) covering workload, role clarity, sense of belonging, mentorship quality, confidence with tasks, and barriers (?sec-annual-review). This turns belonging into data we can act on — and signals that we take the human side of the lab as seriously as the scientific side.






NoteIf you ever feel on the outside



Belonging sometimes wobbles — a new member’s first weeks, a remote member feeling unseen, a hard stretch on a project. If that’s you, say so to your mentor or the PI. Naming it is not a complaint; it’s exactly the kind of early signal this group is built to hear.

Finds and applies for funding and identifies collaborations.
Has members’ backs when they’ve followed the manual, and strives to be impartial.
Chairs lab meetings unless delegated.
Holds final accountability for integrity, authorship, and data governance.



7.2.2 Group Lead / Lab Coordinator
Assists the PI in running the group: coordinating meetings and agendas, overseeing onboarding/offboarding, maintaining shared infrastructure, helping route tasks, and mentoring members. (This role generalizes the former “Lab Manager,” reframed for a hybrid group where the work is data and projects more than benches and reagents.)


7.2.3 Research Assistants / Senior Mentees
Carry out core analysis and writing, mentor more junior members, generate research questions, and help maintain reproducibility standards. Often serve as project leads (below).


7.2.4 Graduate Students
Drive projects, learn methods quickly, mentor undergraduates, generate questions, and pursue professional development they identify themselves as well as opportunities the PI surfaces. Graduate members who complete their degrees may continue with us as Graduate Research Alumni Fellows (below).


7.2.5 Undergraduate Interns / Trainees
Learn skills and procedures, contribute to defined project tasks, and pursue professional development. Every trainee is mentored and mapped to a real deliverable. Trainees who complete their time with us may continue as Research Alumni Fellows (below).


7.2.6 Alumni Fellows and Continuing Collaborators
Completing your time as a trainee does not mean leaving the group. These roles keep alumni connected as continuing contributors and mentors, and they are the living evidence of our through-line’s final stage — Inclusive Workforce Development. Fellow status is recorded in the member directory and confirmed at annual review (?sec-annual-review), so it is always clear who is an active affiliate. Because most fellows are no longer at Lynn University, or affiliated institutions, they are typically mentored and contribute RIPLRT-direct, governed by their current home institution (Section 2.2); their authorship is decided under the same contribution standards as everyone else (Ch. 14), and any data access follows the per-project IRB and data-use terms (?sec-data-governance).

7.2.6.1 Research Alumni Fellows
Former undergraduate trainees (and comparable early-career alumni) who remain affiliated after completing their time with the group. They continue to contribute to manuscripts and projects they helped build, mentor current trainees, and represent the group as they move into graduate study or careers. Typically part-time or remote.


7.2.6.2 Graduate Research Alumni Fellows
Graduate alumni who continue collaborating after completing their degrees. They co-author, advise on methods, help train newer members, and often bridge the group to their new institutions and networks.


7.2.6.3 Postdoctoral Collaborating Mentees and Fellows
Postdoctoral-level collaborators who both receive mentorship — career growth and the path to independence — and provide senior expertise to projects and to junior members. They frequently serve as project leads and co-mentors.



7.2.7 Mentors and Mentees
Mentoring is woven through every role (?sec-mentoring). Mentors are the first line of support for ensuring mentees understand and follow this manual. Alumni fellows are explicitly part of this fabric: they are mentored as they continue to grow, and they mentor those coming up behind them.


7.2.8 Faculty Collaborators
Peer faculty and senior scientists — at Lynn University, the University of Puerto Rico, and other partner institutions — who collaborate on the group’s research as co-investigators, co-PIs, or co-mentors. They contribute scientific direction, domain expertise, data or field sites, and shared mentorship of trainees, and they co-author under the same contribution standards as everyone else (Ch. 14). Collaborators remain governed by their own institutions; where a collaboration involves shared data, human subjects, or funding, the governing IRB, data-use agreement, and entity are confirmed per project (Section 2.2, ?sec-data-governance). Faculty collaborators are partners in the work, not part of the group’s internal reporting line — the role is peer-to-peer.






NoteFlexible, not punitive



This manual replaces the old wage-tier role mechanics (waged/non-waged status changes tied to task completion or precision thresholds) with professional accountability handled through documentation, feedback, and — where applicable — institutional or contractual performance processes (?sec-accountability). Compensation and employment terms are governed by the relevant institution or entity, not by this manual.

title: 7  Roles, Responsibilities, and Project Pod Structure

7.3 The project pod model
A portfolio this size cannot run on one-on-one PI mentoring alone. We organize work into pods: small, project-specific teams with defined roles. Pods distribute leadership, build mentee independence, and protect the PI’s strategic bandwidth — this is training leadership, not distancing from students.
Each pod is chartered using the Project Pod Charter template (/templates/project-pod-charter.qmd) before work begins.

7.3.1 Pod roles
A typical pod assigns these roles (one person may hold more than one; junior members co-hold roles to learn them):

7.3.2 Tiered mentoring within pods
Pods use a senior mentee / project lead → junior mentees → PI oversight structure. The project lead supports junior members day to day; the PI provides scientific oversight and steps in on key decisions (design, authorship, submission). This tiered structure is how we scale mentoring sustainably.


7.3.3 One rule that keeps us healthy






ImportantEvery new member maps to a real deliverable



The group’s risk is not too few people — it is overextension. Every new mentee must map to a funded or near-funded project, a specific deliverable, and a defined supervision pathway before they join a pod. Growth is intentional, aligned with mentoring bandwidth, not maximal.

7.4 Project operating manuals
Each major project (e.g., PR respiratory risk, MESA, AsthmaNet, Framingham/ARIC, All of Us, biomarker projects) maintains a short project operating manual — effectively the completed pod charter plus a two-page operational summary: aims, datasets, access rules, variable dictionary, deliverables, authorship plan, and weekly task structure. These reduce cognitive load and let mentees work more independently.

title: 8  Inclusive Mentoring and Mentee Development
text:
8.1 What inclusive mentoring means here
{#sec-mentoring}
Mentoring is not a side activity at RIPLRT — it is part of the mission. Inclusive workforce development is the final link in our scientific through-line, and mentee co-authorship and growth are documented evidence that we deliver on it. This chapter is our mentoring compact.
Inclusive mentoring means we mentor for the mentee’s trajectory, not only for the project’s output; we recruit and support members with attention to who has historically been excluded from STEM; and we make sure inclusion shows up in our practices, not just our branding.
We recruit and develop members for more than grades or technical skill. We look for and cultivate curiosity, reliability, kindness, willingness to collaborate, a growth mindset, and independent thinking. GPA alone has never built a good scientist.
crumbs: 8  Inclusive Mentoring and Mentee Development

title: 8  Inclusive Mentoring and Mentee Development
text:
8.2 The Mentoring Skills Model
We treat mentoring as a set of learnable skills, not a personality trait — some shared by everyone in a mentoring relationship, some specific to each side of it. We adapt this from the Mentoring Skills Model (Linda Phillips-Jones, PhD), which sorts the skills into three regions.






flowchart LR
    MENTEE["<b>Mentee-Specific Skills</b><br/>Acquiring mentors<br/>Learning quickly<br/>Showing initiative<br/>Following through<br/>Managing the relationship"]
    SHARED["<b>Shared Core Skills</b><br/>Listening actively<br/>Building trust<br/>Encouraging<br/>Identifying goals and current reality"]
    MENTOR["<b>Mentor-Specific Skills</b><br/>Instructing / developing capabilities<br/>Inspiring<br/>Providing corrective feedback<br/>Managing risks<br/>Opening doors"]

    MENTEE --- SHARED --- MENTOR

    classDef core stroke-width:2px;
    class SHARED core;




Figure 8.1: The Mentoring Skills Model — shared core skills practiced by both sides, plus mentee- and mentor-specific skills (adapted from the Mentoring Skills Model, Linda Phillips-Jones, PhD).





Source: https://my.lerner.udel.edu/wp-content/uploads/Skills_for_Sucessful_Mentoring.pdf
As Figure 8.1 shows, the three regions map directly onto how our group works:

Shared core skills — listening actively, building trust, encouraging, and identifying goals and current reality — are the foundation we expect from everyone, in every direction: PI to trainee, peer to peer, alumni fellow to current student, and collaborator to collaborator.
Mentee-specific skills — acquiring mentors, learning quickly, showing initiative, following through, and managing the relationship — are what we actively coach trainees to build. They map onto the development ladder later in this chapter and onto your IDP.
Mentor-specific skills — instructing and developing capabilities, inspiring, providing corrective feedback, managing risks, and opening doors — are what mentors grow into. In our group these are not the PI’s job alone: senior mentees, Graduate Research Alumni Fellows, Postdoctoral Collaborating Mentees and Fellows, and Faculty Collaborators all carry mentor-specific responsibilities (?sec-roles-pods).







TipUse the model in your IDP



At each IDP check-in, name one shared-core skill, one role-specific skill, and one concrete way you will practice each this term. Mentors do the same for their mentor-specific skills. Mentoring is a practice we improve on purpose — not something we assume we already have.


Because the group is built around Inclusive Workforce Development, most members sit on both sides of this model at once: a graduate student is a mentee to the PI and a mentor to an undergraduate; a postdoctoral fellow both receives and provides mentorship. The model is a shared language for getting better at both roles — not a hierarchy.

8.5 The student-development pathway
Mentees grow along a deliberate ladder. The goal is increasing independence and leadership, not just task volume.

8.5.1 Training milestones

Foundation: complete CITI/IRB training as applicable; learn the group’s tools (Git/GitHub, R or Python, the data-governance rules); read this manual.
Contribution: independently own a named deliverable (a figure, a codebook, a literature synthesis, a reproducible notebook).

title: 8  Inclusive Mentoring and Mentee Development
text:
8.6 Mentee co-authorship as mission evidence
We deliberately document trainee co-authorship across abstracts, posters, presentations, and manuscripts. This does double duty: it is genuine scientific output and it is proof of our workforce-development mission — useful in IDPs, grant mentoring plans, training-grant applications, and program reviews. Authorship is governed by the rules in ?sec-authorship; mentees are credited fairly and, where appropriate, on a student-first authorship pathway.
crumbs: 8  Inclusive Mentoring and Mentee Development

title: 8  Inclusive Mentoring and Mentee Development
text:
8.7 Tiered, scalable mentoring
No single person can one-on-one mentor a portfolio this large. We use the tiered pod structure (?sec-roles-pods): senior mentees mentor junior mentees under PI oversight. This both protects bandwidth and gives senior mentees real leadership training. Mentoring others is itself a development milestone.






TipMentoring is reciprocal and developmental



Good mentoring is not the senior person doing the junior person’s thinking. It is structured support that transfers capability. When in doubt, ask: “Did this interaction make my mentee more able to do this independently next time?”
crumbs: 8  Inclusive Mentoring and Mentee Development

title: 8  Inclusive Mentoring and Mentee Development
text:
8.8 Sponsorship vs. mentorship
Mentoring helps people grow; sponsorship uses your standing to open doors for them — nominating them for awards, recommending them for opportunities, putting their name forward when they’re not in the room. RIPLRT mentors are expected to sponsor, not just mentor, as members become ready. Track sponsorship moments in the IDP so they don’t get lost.

title: 9  Lab Culture, Psychological Safety, and Team Science
text:
9.1 Psychological safety is the foundation
{#sec-psych-safety}
Productive science depends as much on human interactions, communication, and group dynamics as on technical excellence. This chapter describes the culture we are building and the specific practices that protect it.
Psychological safety means members feel able to ask naive questions, admit they don’t know something, surface mistakes early, and disagree with the PI — without fear of looking foolish or paying a price. It is the single strongest predictor of whether a team learns and performs.
For a group where people are learning coding, statistics, and environmental-health methods at the same time, this is non-negotiable. We normalize “learning in public”:
crumbs: 9  Lab Culture, Psychological Safety, and Team Science

title: 9  Lab Culture, Psychological Safety, and Team Science
text:
Questions are contributions. The person asking the “obvious” question is usually asking what three others were thinking.
Mistakes surfaced early are cheap; mistakes hidden are expensive. We thank people for catching errors — including their own.
Disagreement with the PI or senior members is welcome and expected. Good science needs dissent.
crumbs: 9  Lab Culture, Psychological Safety, and Team Science

title: 9  Lab Culture, Psychological Safety, and Team Science
text:
9.2 Leaders set the norms
Members emulate leadership behavior. The PI and senior members must model the culture they want — especially in the moments that test it: during authorship discussions, revisions, disagreements, and deadline pressure. If we want a team that is direct, rigorous, collaborative, and fair, leadership has to be visibly direct, rigorous, collaborative, and fair first.
Concretely, leaders:

Admit their own mistakes and uncertainty out loud.
Solicit input before stating their own view, so they don’t anchor the room.
Resist dominating discussion; senior scientists can crowd out everyone else without meaning to.
Give credit generously and specifically.
crumbs: 9  Lab Culture, Psychological Safety, and Team Science

title: 9  Lab Culture, Psychological Safety, and Team Science
text:
9.3 Team science, by design
We work across disciplines, institutions, datasets, and time zones. That requires intentional team-science practice:

Shared narrative. The Community-to-Clinic-to-Cloud story is the operating narrative that lets people on different datasets feel part of one program.
Clear interfaces. Pod charters and the project pod model define who owns what, so collaboration doesn’t dissolve into “who’s doing this?”
Co-mentoring and distributed capacity. We draw on collaborators’ expertise rather than pretending any one person knows everything.
Delegation as development. We deliberately hand off lab-meeting leadership, journal-club facilitation, figure ownership, codebook stewardship, literature synthesis, and dashboard building. Delegation builds trust and motivation — and trains leaders.
crumbs: 9  Lab Culture, Psychological Safety, and Team Science

title: 9  Lab Culture, Psychological Safety, and Team Science
text:
9.4 Meetings that invite participation
Meetings are where culture is most visible. Ours are designed so junior members speak, question data, and critique safely.

Rotating roles. Facilitator, note-taker, and “first question” rotate so the same voices don’t always lead.
Structured turns. We make space for students to present and to ask questions before senior members weigh in.
Safe critique. We critique the work, not the person, and we praise good questions as much as good answers.
Wins & roadblocks. A recurring segment surfaces both progress and stuck points without stigma.

(See ?sec-communication for channels, cadence, and agenda templates.)
crumbs: 9  Lab Culture, Psychological Safety, and Team Science

title: 9  Lab Culture, Psychological Safety, and Team Science
section: 9.5 Inclusion is part of the culture, not the branding
text:
9.5 Inclusion is part of the culture, not the branding
Leaders shape cultures that recognize and eliminate discriminatory or harassing behavior. This aligns directly with our mission to broaden participation in STEM. Inclusion shows up here in concrete practices: equitable recruitment, rotating visible roles, attention to who speaks and who is credited, bilingual communication, and a low-friction path to raise concerns (?sec-accountability). We do not tolerate harassment or discrimination of any kind (see CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).
crumbs: 9  Lab Culture, Psychological Safety, and Team Science

title: 9  Lab Culture, Psychological Safety, and Team Science
section: 9.6 We evaluate the lab as a human system
text:
9.6 We evaluate the lab as a human system
We already evaluate projects scientifically. We also evaluate the group as a human system. Each quarter we run a brief, anonymous lab climate check covering workload, clarity, belonging, mentorship quality, confidence, and barriers. Each year we run a fuller stop / start / continue review (?sec-annual-review). Self-awareness, feedback, and adaptation are leadership responsibilities, not optional extras.






TipThe one-line test for our culture



Can the most junior person in the room disagree with the most senior person about the data — and have it go well? If yes, the culture is working. If you’re ever unsure, that’s worth raising.

We use several streams, each with a clear purpose. If communication styles differ across the group, we revisit these after a trial period rather than forcing one channel to do everything.

10.3 File naming and document hygiene

All shared documents live in the RIPLRT shared drive (or the project repo for code). Even a first solo draft is created in the shared space — transparency and open collaboration are foundational.
Follow the file-naming convention for each folder. Where a folder has a README describing its naming pattern, follow it; if one is missing, ask the project lead or PI and add one.

title: 10  Communication, Meetings, and Digital Body Language
text:
10.4 Meeting cadence

Weekly pod check-ins keep projects moving; use the weekly agenda template.
A recurring group huddle (“RIPLRT Wins & Roadblocks”) builds identity across members on different datasets.
One-on-one mentoring meetings run biweekly (see ?sec-mentoring).
Day, time, and frequency adapt to members’ real availability; keep your availability current so scheduling is honest.

Every meeting has an agenda in advance and notes + action items after (owner + due date), stored in the tracked tool. No agenda, no meeting; no notes, no follow-through.

title: 10  Communication, Meetings, and Digital Body Language
text:
10.5 Digital body language
Tone is hard to read in text, and the absence of cues (face, voice, pauses) means people fill gaps with assumptions — usually negative ones. Digital body language is the set of signals our written communication sends. We are deliberate about it.
Practices we use:

Acknowledge receipt. A quick “got it, will reply by Thursday” prevents silence from reading as dismissal.
Match channel to weight. Hard or sensitive conversations move to a call. Bad news and conflict are not for chat threads.
Be generous in interpretation, careful in expression. Assume good intent when reading; reduce ambiguity when writing.
Mind asynchronous timing. A message sent at 11 PM should not imply a reply is expected at 11 PM. Use scheduled send or a “no rush” note. Respect availability and time off.
Watch the curtness gap. Brevity that feels efficient to the sender can read as cold to the receiver. A little warmth (a greeting, a thank-you, a sign-off) is not inefficiency; it’s maintenance of trust.
Punctuation and response time carry meaning. A one-word reply, a long delay, or a sudden formality shift all signal something. If you notice these in others, check in rather than assume; if you’re sending them, consider what they convey.







NoteRead for signal, not just content



When a teammate’s messages change — terser, slower, more formal, suddenly cc’ing others — treat it as information. It often means stress, confusion, or a problem surfacing. The right move is a kind, direct check-in (“Hey, want to hop on a quick call about this?”), not a tit-for-tat escalation in writing.
crumbs: 10  Communication, Meetings, and Digital Body Language

title: 10  Communication, Meetings, and Digital Body Language
text:
10.6 No-surprises communication
The single most important communication norm at RIPLRT: no surprises.

If a deadline is at risk, say so early and propose a renegotiation — don’t go silent and miss it.
If an analysis isn’t working, raise it before the meeting, not in front of the room cold.
If you’re overloaded, name it before it becomes a crisis.

Communicating a problem early is a sign of professionalism, not failure. The version of you that says “I’m going to be two days late, here’s my plan” is far more trusted than the version that misses silently and explains afterward.

11.3 Task hygiene
A task is only real if it has:

An owner (one person, even if others help).
A due date (or an explicit “no date — backlog” status).
A definition of done (what the deliverable is).
A link to where the work lives (repo, doc, or board).

We review the board in weekly check-ins: what shipped, what’s blocked, what’s next. Blocked tasks get surfaced early — “no surprises.”

title: 11  Project Management and Workflow Systems
text:
11.4 Managing the portfolio without overload
The portfolio spans population-scale surveillance to molecular modeling. To keep it sane:

Pods, not heroics. Work is distributed across pods with defined roles (?sec-roles-pods), not concentrated on one or two people.
Project operating manuals. Each major project keeps a two-page operational summary so anyone can orient quickly and mentees can work independently.
One lead metric per goal. Per the IAP cadence, each strategic goal carries a single lead metric so progress is legible.
Quarterly review rhythm. We score progress against milestones each quarter (?sec-annual-review) and re-plan rather than letting work drift.
crumbs: 11  Project Management and Workflow Systems

title: 11  Project Management and Workflow Systems
text:
11.5 Aligning daily work to strategy
Project work should ladder up to the group’s SMART goals (the 12/36/60-month roadmap in the IAP). In practice:

Each pod’s deliverables map to a named SMART goal (e.g., “RespRisk v1.0 forecasting workflow,” “manuscript pipeline,” “mentee-integrated production”).
When prioritizing, we ask: does this advance a SMART goal and the through-line? If a request doesn’t, it goes to the backlog or gets declined — protecting time for the work that matters most.

title: 12  Data Governance, IRB, Privacy, and Responsible Research
text: Access is a privilege tied to training, approval, and need. We collect the minimum, protect it rigorously, and honor every agreement that lets us use it.

title: 12  Data Governance, IRB, Privacy, and Responsible Research
text:
12.2 Human-subjects training and IRB
Before touching any human-subjects data (including tissues, raw data, or derived data), you must:

Complete and maintain CITI Program training appropriate to your role — typically Biomedical Research (Basic), Responsible Conduct of Research, Data or Specimens, Conflicts of Interest, and Information Privacy for Researchers. Add bloodborne-pathogen training if any biospecimen work applies.
Be added by name to the approved IRB protocol for your project. If you are not on the protocol, you cannot access the data or participate in the project — no exceptions.
Confirm the IRB-of-record for your project (it varies by institution and partnership).







ImportantPlaceholder: IRB and training specifics



The IRB-of-record, protocol numbers, CITI institutional affiliation, and required module list must be confirmed per project with the PI. Links and exact requirements are recorded in each project’s pod charter. Do not assume; ask.
crumbs: 12  Data Governance, IRB, Privacy, and Responsible Research

title: 12  Data Governance, IRB, Privacy, and Responsible Research
text:
12.3 Dataset-specific rules
Each dataset we use carries its own Data Use Agreement (DUA) and access rules. These are not interchangeable. Common examples:







Resource
Typical governance considerations




PR DoH / ASES claims & pharmacy
DUA terms, de-identification, approved analysts only, secure environment


BioLINCC
Application, DUA, data security plan, no re-identification, citation requirements


BioData Catalyst / All of Us Workbench
Cloud workspace, registered/controlled tiers, no data egress, workbench-only analysis


MESA, Framingham, AsthmaNet, NHANES
Repository-specific use terms, acknowledgment language, redistribution limits



The Data Steward for each pod owns compliance with that project’s DUA. Before you analyze, confirm with the steward: What tier is this? Where must analysis happen? What can leave the environment? What must be cited or acknowledged?
Use the Data-Use and Access Checklist (/templates/data-use-access-checklist.qmd) at the start of every project.
crumbs: 12  Data Governance, IRB, Privacy, and Responsible Research

title: 12  Data Governance, IRB, Privacy, and Responsible Research
text:
12.4 De-identification and HIPAA-adjacent thinking
Even when data are de-identified, we treat them with care:

Never attempt re-identification of any individual, ever.
Apply de-identification standards (e.g., removing or transforming direct identifiers; respecting small-cell suppression so individuals can’t be inferred).
Report results at aggregate levels that protect individuals; watch out for small cells in stratified (equity) analyses.
Treat claims, pharmacy, and clinical data as HIPAA-adjacent: handle them with the caution you’d give protected health information even when a project is technically outside HIPAA’s direct scope.
crumbs: 12  Data Governance, IRB, Privacy, and Responsible Research

title: 12  Data Governance, IRB, Privacy, and Responsible Research
text:
12.5 Access control and secure storage

Least privilege: people get access only to what their role requires.
No restricted data in general channels. Never put restricted or identifiable data in chat, email, personal drives, personal laptops, or public repos.
Analyze where the agreement says to. For controlled-tier repositories, analysis stays inside the approved workbench/environment; no downloading or egress unless explicitly permitted.
Secrets stay out of code. No credentials, tokens, or keys in GitHub. Use environment variables and a .gitignore that excludes data and secrets.
Encryption and backups follow institutional policy for any local handling that is permitted.
crumbs: 12  Data Governance, IRB, Privacy, and Responsible Research

title: 12  Data Governance, IRB, Privacy, and Responsible Research
text:
12.6 Privacy of people — including us

No photos or videos of human research participants, ever — that violates privacy and IRB rules.
Photos/videos of group members require consent before capture, and any public posting requires PI approval.
Respect the privacy of community partners and participants in everything we publish or post.
crumbs: 12  Data Governance, IRB, Privacy, and Responsible Research

title: 12  Data Governance, IRB, Privacy, and Responsible Research
text:
12.7 Responsible research conduct

No fabrication, falsification, or plagiarism. A negative result is still a result.
Document analyses so they are reproducible (?sec-reproducible); reproducibility is a privacy-and-integrity control, not just a quality one.
Disclose conflicts of interest per institutional policy.
Follow sponsor terms and data-sharing/publication requirements of each dataset and grant.


12.7.1 Which institution governs your data
Before you request or touch any dataset, know which umbrella you are working under (Section 2.2) — it sets which IRB, training, and data-use agreement apply.








Your umbrella
IRB of record
Training & agreements




EBDL / Lynn University
Lynn University IRB

UPR-affiliated
UPR IRB (or reliance, as applicable)
UPR CITI/IRB listing; collaboration/DUA terms 


RIPLRT / LLC (non-Lynn, non-UPR)
Protocol named in the project charter
Sponsor terms + LLC data-use rules



When a project spans institutions (e.g., a Lynn member analyzing UPR-sourceddata), the most restrictive applicable terms govern, and the data-use agreement controls. When in doubt, ask the PI before access is provisioned.

title: 12  Data Governance, IRB, Privacy, and Responsible Research
text:
12.8 When something goes wrong
If you suspect a data breach, an access error, a consent problem, or a possible integrity issue:

Stop the activity in question.
Tell the PI and the Data Steward immediately — early reporting protects you and the people in the data.
Document what happened factually.

This is explicitly a no-blame, report-early expectation. The only serious mistake is hiding the problem.

title: 13  Reproducible Science, Open Science, and Version Control
text: If it isn’t reproducible, it isn’t finished. Anyone in the group should be able to clone a project, restore the environment, and regenerate every figure, table, and number in a manuscript from raw inputs.
crumbs: 13  Reproducible Science, Open Science, and Version Control

title: 13  Reproducible Science, Open Science, and Version Control
section: 13.2 Version control with Git and GitHub
text:
13.2 Version control with Git and GitHub
All code lives in Git, hosted on GitHub under the RIPLRT organization. No exceptions, no “I’ll add it later,” no analysis living only on a laptop.
Workflow basics:

Work on branches, not directly on main.
Commit early and often with clear messages (fix: correct lag window in DLM, not stuff).
Open pull requests for review; analysis code gets a second set of eyes before it shapes a result.
Use issues to track bugs, questions, and tasks.
Never commit data, credentials, or secrets — enforce with .gitignore.

Use the GitHub Repository Checklist (/templates/github-repo-checklist.qmd) when setting up any new project.






ImportantConsult before going public



Before making any repository, dataset, or notebook public, confirm with the PI or project lead. Public release must respect DUAs, IRB terms, embargoes, and authorship plans (this rule is inherited from the original manual and still applies).
crumbs: 13  Reproducible Science, Open Science, and Version Control

title: 13  Reproducible Science, Open Science, and Version Control
text:
13.3 Reproducible analysis with Quarto
We author analysis and manuscripts in Quarto (modernizing the group’s earlier R Markdown / Bookdown practice). Quarto lets prose, code, and output live together and render to HTML, PDF, and Word.
Standards:

Analyses are literate: code, narrative, and results in one document.
Computational environments are captured — use renv (R) or a lockfile / requirements.txt/environment.yml (Python) so versions are pinned.
Set a random seed for any stochastic step.
Documents render cleanly from scratch (use Quarto’s freeze thoughtfully, but verify a clean render before milestones).
Paths are relative, never absolute (data/ not /Users/you/Desktop/...).

Run the Reproducible Analysis Checklist (/templates/reproducible-analysis-checklist.qmd) before any submission.
crumbs: 13  Reproducible Science, Open Science, and Version Control

title: 13  Reproducible Science, Open Science, and Version Control
text:
13.4 Project repository structure
A consistent skeleton makes every project legible:
project-name/
├── README.md            # what this is, how to run it
├── data/                # raw/ (gitignored), interim/, processed/
├── R/  or  src/         # functions and scripts
├── analysis/            # numbered Quarto notebooks
├── outputs/             # figures/, tables/, dashboards/
├── docs/                # manuscripts, briefs
├── renv.lock / env.yml  # pinned environment
└── .gitignore           # excludes data, secrets, large files

Raw data is read-only and never edited by hand — all cleaning is scripted, so it’s reproducible and auditable.
Number notebooks (01-clean.qmd, 02-model.qmd) so the pipeline order is obvious.
crumbs: 13  Reproducible Science, Open Science, and Version Control

title: 13  Reproducible Science, Open Science, and Version Control
text:
13.5 Open science
We contribute to open science deliberately, within what agreements allow:

Preregister analysis plans on OSF where appropriate — especially for forecasting work, to separate confirmatory from exploratory analysis.
Archive curated code and (permissible) data with DOIs via Zenodo or FigShare.
Share reproducible notebooks and manuscripts open-access where possible.
Re-analyzing public datasets is good open science, not plagiarism — it advances reproducibility.







NoteOpen by default, closed by necessity



Our bias is toward openness and transparency. But openness never overrides a data-use agreement, IRB term, participant privacy, or an embargo. When the two seem to conflict, governance wins and you ask the PI.
crumbs: 13  Reproducible Science, Open Science, and Version Control

title: 13  Reproducible Science, Open Science, and Version Control
text:
13.6 Reproducibility as mentoring
Building a reproducible pipeline is one of the most valuable things a mentee learns here. It is also a deliverable in its own right: a clean, documented, reproducible notebook is a legitimate scholarly product and a strong portfolio piece. We credit reproducibility work like the real work it is (?sec-authorship).

title: 14  Responsible Use of AI in Research and Writing
crumbs: 14  Responsible Use of AI in Research and Writing

title: 14  Responsible Use of AI in Research and Writing
text: AI accelerates judgment; it never replaces it. You are fully responsible for everything you submit, regardless of which tools helped you make it.
crumbs: 14  Responsible Use of AI in Research and Writing

title: 14  Responsible Use of AI in Research and Writing
text:
14.2 Where AI helps (encouraged, with care)

Coding: scaffolding functions, debugging, explaining errors, drafting tests. You read, understand, and verify every line before it enters a pipeline.
Writing: brainstorming structure, tightening prose, drafting non-results sections, improving clarity and bilingual phrasing. You own the claims, the citations, and the voice.
Literature synthesis: orienting to a new area, surfacing search terms, summarizing papers you then read.
Workflow automation: drafting scripts, templates, and documentation.


14.2.1 AI tools and data across umbrellas
Which AI tools you may use — and which data you may put into them — depends on your umbrella (Section 2.2) and the data-governance rules (?sec-data-governance):

EBDL / Lynn members use AI tools approved under Lynn University policy and may process Lynn-governed or IRB-listed data only in environments Lynn permits.
RIPLRT / LLC infrastructure — including tools built by FERM Technologies (the LLC’s technology DBA) — is governed by LLC and sponsor terms, not by default Lynn approvals. 
UPR or external members follow their home institution’s AI and data rules.

Do not move data, prompts, or model outputs across umbrellas without explicit authorization — putting Lynn-governed or UPR-governed data into an LLC tool (or vice versa) is a data-governance event, not a convenience. Disclose AI assistance per this chapter regardless of which umbrella’s tools you used.
crumbs: 14  Responsible Use of AI in Research and Writing

title: 14  Responsible Use of AI in Research and Writing
text:
14.3 Where AI must not go (prohibited)






ImportantHard limits




Never paste restricted, identifiable, IRB-governed, claims, pharmacy, clinical, or DUA-controlled data into any external AI tool. This is a data-governance violation (?sec-data-governance). Treat AI prompt boxes as public.
Never present AI-generated text or analysis as verified fact without checking it. LLMs fabricate citations, statistics, and results convincingly.
Never let AI fabricate, alter, or “clean up” data or results. That is research misconduct.
Never submit AI-written work you do not understand and cannot defend. If you can’t explain it, you can’t submit it.
crumbs: 14  Responsible Use of AI in Research and Writing

title: 14  Responsible Use of AI in Research and Writing
text:
14.4 Verify everything
AI output is a draft to be checked, never a source of truth:

Citations: confirm every reference exists, says what’s claimed, and is correctly attributed. AI invents plausible-looking citations.
Numbers and stats: re-derive or independently verify any quantitative claim.
Code: read it, test it, and confirm it does what you think on real cases.
Facts and methods: cross-check against primary sources.
crumbs: 14  Responsible Use of AI in Research and Writing

title: 14  Responsible Use of AI in Research and Writing
text:
14.5 Disclosure and transparency
We are transparent about AI use, both internally and in what we publish:

Internally: note material AI assistance in commit messages, notebooks, or the relevant doc so collaborators know what was AI-assisted and what was human-verified.
For scholarly products: follow the AI-Use Disclosure template and the disclosure requirements of the target journal, conference, or sponsor. Many venues require statements about AI use; some prohibit certain uses. Check before submitting.
AI tools are not authors. They cannot take responsibility for the work, so they do not meet authorship criteria (?sec-authorship).
crumbs: 14  Responsible Use of AI in Research and Writing

title: 14  Responsible Use of AI in Research and Writing
text:
14.6 AI and student work
For mentees, AI is a learning accelerator and a learning hazard. Our stance:

AI is allowed for learning, drafting, and debugging — as a tutor and assistant, not a substitute for developing skill.
The goal of training is your capability. If AI does the thinking you were supposed to learn, you’ve been shortchanged. Use it to go faster on things you already understand and to learn things you then internalize.
Mentors and mentees discuss AI use openly in IDPs and one-on-ones — what’s helping, what’s becoming a crutch.
crumbs: 14  Responsible Use of AI in Research and Writing

title: 14  Responsible Use of AI in Research and Writing
text:
14.7 Why we hold this line
Our credibility — with reviewers, partners, communities, and sponsors — rests on integrity and reproducibility. Equity-focused work especially cannot afford fabricated results or leaked data. Responsible AI use protects the people in our data, the trust of our partners, and the development of our trainees. Speed is never worth a shortcut on any of those.






TipThe defensibility test



Before submitting anything AI helped with, ask: Could I explain and defend every claim, line of code, and citation here to the PI or a reviewer, as if no AI were involved? If yes, proceed. If no, you’re not done.
crumbs: 14  Responsible Use of AI in Research and Writing

title: 15  Authorship, Contributorship, Presentations, and Public Dissemination
text:
ICMJE governs authorship. We follow the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors criteria.
CRediT documents contributorship. We use a CRediT-style taxonomy to record who did what.
Authorship is discussed at the start of every project, not negotiated at the end. Surprises about credit are exactly the kind of “surprise” our culture forbids.
Mentees are credited fairly, including on a student-first authorship pathway where appropriate.


15.1.1 Institutional affiliations on bylines and disclosures
Your byline affiliation reflects your home institution, not the Institute’s parent entity (Section 2.2):

Lynn-affiliated members — list Lynn University (and the Educational Biomarker Discovery Lab where a lab affiliation is appropriate).
UPR-affiliated members — list the University of Puerto Rico unit youbelong to.
The PI lists his Lynn University appointment and, where appropriate, the RIPLRT Institute / Felix E. Rivera-Mariani, PhD, LLC.
Independent or external members without a current institution — coordinate affiliation with the PI; “RIPLRT Institute” may serve as the
research-group affiliation.

Do not list “Lynn University” for a member who is not Lynn-affiliated, and do not imply that the RIPLRT Institute is a Lynn University unit. Acknowledgments and funding disclosures name the entity that actually held the award or provided the resource — Lynn-administered grant, LLC/RIPLRT, sponsor, or UPR — not a default.
crumbs: 15  Authorship, Contributorship, Presentations, and Public Dissemination

title: 15  Authorship, Contributorship, Presentations, and Public Dissemination
text:
15.2 ICMJE authorship criteria
To be an author, a person must meet all four ICMJE criteria:

Substantial contributions to conception/design, or acquisition, analysis, or interpretation of data; and
Drafting the work or revising it critically for important intellectual content; and
Final approval of the version to be published; and
Agreement to be accountable for all aspects of the work.

Contributors who do not meet all four are acknowledged, not listed as authors. Meeting only one criterion (e.g., funding, or only collecting data) does not by itself confer authorship.
crumbs: 15  Authorship, Contributorship, Presentations, and Public Dissemination

title: 15  Authorship, Contributorship, Presentations, and Public Dissemination
text:
15.3 CRediT contributorship taxonomy
For each product we record contributions using CRediT roles, which makes credit specific and visible: Conceptualization, Methodology, Software, Validation, Formal analysis, Investigation, Resources, Data curation, Writing – original draft, Writing – review & editing, Visualization, Supervision, Project administration, Funding acquisition.
Map pod roles to CRediT contributions in the Authorship/Contributorship Agreement (/templates/authorship-contributorship-agreement.qmd) at project start, and update it as roles evolve.
crumbs: 15  Authorship, Contributorship, Presentations, and Public Dissemination

title: 15  Authorship, Contributorship, Presentations, and Public Dissemination
section: 15.4 Author order and the student-first pathway
text:
15.4 Author order and the student-first pathway

First author: led the intellectual and practical work of the product — often the project’s analysis or writing lead, frequently a mentee.
Senior/last author: the PI or supervising scientist who provided direction and accountability.
Middle authors: ordered by contribution, discussed openly.
Student-first pathway: when a mentee has done the lead work, they earn first authorship. Building mentees into first- and co-first-author positions is a documented goal of this group (it appears in the IAP SMART goals) and a deliberate feature of our workforce-development mission.







NoteDisagreements about credit



Authorship disputes are handled early and directly, mediated by the PI, with reference to the documented contributorship agreement. Because we write the plan down at the start and update it as we go, most disputes are prevented rather than resolved. AI tools are never authors (?sec-responsible-ai).
crumbs: 15  Authorship, Contributorship, Presentations, and Public Dissemination

title: 15  Authorship, Contributorship, Presentations, and Public Dissemination
text:
15.5 Presentations, posters, and conferences

Every member is expected to present ongoing research at least once a year — mentees at a regional or (preferably) national conference aligned with their goals.
Presenting authorship follows the same fairness principles; the presenter is typically the person who led the work.
Use the Conference Abstract Planning Sheet (/templates/conference-abstract-planning.qmd) and confirm the authorship list before submission.
We actively pursue travel awards and scholarships so cost is not a barrier (?sec-funding).
crumbs: 15  Authorship, Contributorship, Presentations, and Public Dissemination

title: 15  Authorship, Contributorship, Presentations, and Public Dissemination
text:
15.6 Public dissemination and science communication
Our mission requires translating science beyond journals:

Clinician-facing dashboards, community risk briefs, public-health playbooks, and bilingual science-communication content are first-class products (?sec-research-products), and contributors to them are credited.
Public-facing materials (including social media via the group’s science-communication channels) get PI review before release, must respect data governance and privacy, and represent the group and its partners responsibly.
Bilingual (Spanish/English) communication is a core value; community materials should reach the communities they’re about.
crumbs: 15  Authorship, Contributorship, Presentations, and Public Dissemination

title: 15  Authorship, Contributorship, Presentations, and Public Dissemination
text:
15.7 Strategic, non-defensive framing
When we describe our own work — in talks, briefs, bios, or proposals — we lead with credentials and institutional value, not personal advancement, and we frame new work as a forward progression from prior work rather than a reprise. Self-promotion is fine; it should simply be credential-forward and self-decentered, able to survive scrutiny without sounding defensive. This protects both the science and the group’s reputation.
crumbs: 15  Authorship, Contributorship, Presentations, and Public Dissemination

title: 15  Authorship, Contributorship, Presentations, and Public Dissemination
text:
15.8 Acknowledgments and funding

Acknowledge funders, data providers, and repositories using the exact language each requires (BioLINCC, All of Us, MESA, etc. each specify acknowledgment text).
Acknowledge non-author contributors (with their permission).
Report conflicts of interest per venue and institutional policy.

16.1.1 Ownership of research products
Datasets, code, dashboards, models, and other products carry ownership and intellectual-property (IP) implications that follow the umbrella under which they were created and the resources used (Section 2.2). Get this right before a product with potential value is built.
General principles (confirm specifics before relying on them):

16.2 Manuscripts

Start with the Manuscript Planning Sheet: target journal, key message, figures, authorship plan, and timeline — before drafting.
One Writing Lead coordinates drafting and submission; sections are delegated to build skills (figure lead, methods lead, literature-synthesis lead).
Every number and figure traces back to a reproducible notebook (?sec-reproducible).
Aim for the IAP cadence: a steady, thematically coherent manuscript pipeline organized around our four themes — aeroallergen/fungal early-warning science; respiratory severity and care pathways; biomarker/microbiome signatures; and equity-stratified environmental risk.

title: 16  Research Products: Manuscripts, Abstracts, Posters, Dashboards, and Briefs

16.3 Abstracts and posters

Abstracts are often a mentee’s first scholarly product — treat them as real training, not filler.
Maintain a shared abstract calendar of society deadlines (AAAAI, AAI, ATS, SOT, ASM, ISES, ASBMB, ABRCMS, and others).
Posters reuse manuscript figures and the through-line narrative; keep a poster template and the group’s visual identity in /assets.
Confirm authorship before submission; rehearse presentations as a pod.

title: 16  Research Products: Manuscripts, Abstracts, Posters, Dashboards, and Briefs

16.4 Dashboards and decision-support tools
Forecasting and decision tools (e.g., the RespRisk line described in the IAP) are flagship products:

Build them reproducibly, with documented thresholds, fairness/equity checks, and clear risk tiers (e.g., green/amber/red).
Co-develop with stakeholders; validate against real-world outcomes; report calibration, decision-curve utility, and equity-stratified performance.
Version dashboards like code; never expose restricted data through a tool.

16.5 Community briefs and bilingual communication
These close the Community-to-Clinic-to-Cloud loop:

Community risk briefs translate forecasts into plain-language, actionable summaries for the communities the data come from.
Materials are bilingual (Spanish/English) so they reach the people they’re about.
Briefs get PI review and respect privacy and partner relationships.
Track real-world uptake (briefs issued, decisions supported, partner adoption) — impact is a product too.

title: 16  Research Products: Manuscripts, Abstracts, Posters, Dashboards, and Briefs

16.6 Quality bar for every product
Before anything leaves the group:

It is reproducible (or, for non-analytic products, traceable to reproducible work).
It respects data governance, privacy, and DUAs.
Its authorship/contributorship is documented and agreed.
It has been reviewed (peer within the pod + PI as appropriate).
It advances a SMART goal and the through-line — we make products on purpose, not just to be busy.







TipProducts are also development



Match products to mentees’ growth. A first abstract, a first figure, a first reproducible notebook, a first first-authorship — each is both a research output and a rung on the development ladder (?sec-mentoring). Plan products with people’s growth in mind, not just the project’s needs.

title: 17  Health, Safety, Fieldwork, Biospecimens, and Remote Work
text:
17.1 General principle
This chapter replaces the original manual’s COVID-specific section with a broader, durable policy covering the range of settings our hybrid group works in: remote and home offices, fieldwork and community sites, any biospecimen handling, and shared facilities. It also retains a flexible public-health protocol for when one is needed.
crumbs: 17  Health, Safety, Fieldwork, Biospecimens, and Remote Work

title: 17  Health, Safety, Fieldwork, Biospecimens, and Remote Work
text: Your health and safety come first. No deadline, dataset, or deliverable is worth your wellbeing. Tell the PI or your mentor about any health or safety concern — including allergies or conditions that affect your work — so we can support you.
crumbs: 17  Health, Safety, Fieldwork, Biospecimens, and Remote Work

title: 17  Health, Safety, Fieldwork, Biospecimens, and Remote Work
text:
17.2 Remote and hybrid work
Most of our work is computational and can be done remotely. To make remote work healthy and effective:

Ergonomics matter. Set up a workspace that protects your eyes, wrists, and back; take regular breaks.
Sustainable hours. We do not measure worth by hours online. Get the work done well; protect rest and boundaries (?sec-funding covers wellbeing and burnout prevention more fully).
Availability, not surveillance. Keep your availability current so work is planned realistically; we trust members to manage their time. (We do not use geo-location time-tracking; that practice from the wet-lab era is retired.)
Security travels with you. Remote work follows the same data-governance rules (?sec-data-governance): no restricted data on personal devices or unsecured networks; analyze controlled data only in approved environments.
Stay connected. Remote members are deliberately included in meetings, decisions, authorship, and the social life of the group (?sec-belonging).
crumbs: 17  Health, Safety, Fieldwork, Biospecimens, and Remote Work

title: 17  Health, Safety, Fieldwork, Biospecimens, and Remote Work
text:
17.3 Fieldwork and community sites
When work happens in communities, partner clinics, or field settings:

Plan and brief first. Confirm site contacts, logistics, consent procedures, and an emergency plan before going.
Respect community partners. We are guests; follow partner site rules and cultural norms. Communities are collaborators, not subjects.
Never photograph or record research participants (?sec-data-governance). Capture only what consent and IRB allow.
Travel safely. Follow institutional travel and safety policies; don’t work alone in unfamiliar settings without a check-in plan.
Protect data in transit. Field-collected data follows the same security and de-identification rules from the moment it’s captured.
crumbs: 17  Health, Safety, Fieldwork, Biospecimens, and Remote Work

title: 17  Health, Safety, Fieldwork, Biospecimens, and Remote Work
text:
17.4 Biospecimens (when applicable)
If a project involves biological specimens (human blood, tissue, or environmental bioaerosol samples):

Complete required bloodborne-pathogen and biosafety training and maintain relevant vaccinations (e.g., Hepatitis B) per institutional policy when handling human blood/fluids.
Follow the biosafety level, PPE, and handling procedures for the facility and protocol.
Label, store, log, and chain-of-custody specimens per the protocol; never improvise.
Dispose of biological and chemical waste per institutional and regulatory rules.
Wear appropriate PPE and follow facility dress/safety codes when in a lab space.







NotePlaceholder: facility-specific safety rules



Exact biosafety levels, PPE requirements, vaccination/clearance rules, waste procedures, and emergency contacts depend on the specific facility and institution. These must be confirmed locally before any wet-lab or biospecimen work and recorded in the project’s operating manual.
crumbs: 17  Health, Safety, Fieldwork, Biospecimens, and Remote Work

title: 17  Health, Safety, Fieldwork, Biospecimens, and Remote Work
text:
17.5 Public-health and infectious-disease protocol (flexible)
Rather than a single pandemic-specific section, we keep a scalable protocol that activates when public-health conditions require it (a respiratory illness surge, a new advisory, fieldwork in an outbreak area):

Follow current institutional, local, state, and federal guidance — that guidance, not this manual, is authoritative and current.
The PI may activate measures proportionate to the situation: remote-first work, masking, distancing, capacity limits in shared spaces, testing, or pausing in-person activity.
Stay home when sick; we would always rather you rest than risk others. Sickness is never penalized.
For fieldwork during an active outbreak, add a site-specific risk assessment to the project operating manual.
crumbs: 17  Health, Safety, Fieldwork, Biospecimens, and Remote Work

title: 17  Health, Safety, Fieldwork, Biospecimens, and Remote Work
text:
17.6 Reporting incidents
Report any injury, exposure, near-miss, safety concern, or health-and-safety question to the PI promptly. Reporting is expected and never penalized — early reporting keeps everyone safe.
