title: 18  Conflict Resolution, Feedback, and Accountability
crumbs: 18  Conflict Resolution, Feedback, and Accountability

title: 18  Conflict Resolution, Feedback, and Accountability
text: We address problems early, directly, and kindly. We separate the person from the problem. We assume good faith. And we document, so accountability is fair and clear.
crumbs: 18  Conflict Resolution, Feedback, and Accountability

title: 18  Conflict Resolution, Feedback, and Accountability
text:
18.2 Feedback culture
Feedback is a routine, two-directional habit — not a rare, high-stakes event.

Frequent and specific. Small, timely feedback beats a once-a-year verdict. “Specifically, the lag window in this model needs justification” beats “be more rigorous.”
Kind and candid. Care personally and challenge directly. Withholding honest feedback to be “nice” is neither kind nor helpful.
Two-way. Mentees give feedback to mentors and the PI, including in anonymous climate checks. Leaders model receiving feedback well.
About the work. We critique ideas, code, and drafts — never the worth of the person.

Use the Stop / Start / Continue Feedback Form (/templates/stop-start-continue.qmd) in one-on-ones and reviews.
crumbs: 18  Conflict Resolution, Feedback, and Accountability

title: 18  Conflict Resolution, Feedback, and Accountability
section: 18.3 A structured way to handle difficult conversations
text:
18.3 A structured way to handle difficult conversations
When a conversation is hard, it helps to separate three things people usually tangle together:

What happened. Get curious about each person’s account before deciding who’s “right.” There are usually two reasonable stories. Ask, don’t assume.
Feelings. Name the emotions in play (yours and theirs) instead of letting them leak into the content. Frustration unacknowledged becomes blame.
Identity. Notice what the conflict says to each person about themselves (“Am I competent? Am I respected?”). Many conflicts escalate because an identity feels threatened, not because the facts are far apart.

Naming these explicitly — even just to yourself before the conversation — defuses most of the heat.
crumbs: 18  Conflict Resolution, Feedback, and Accountability

title: 18  Conflict Resolution, Feedback, and Accountability
text:
18.4 Practical conflict-resolution steps





flowchart TB
    A[Notice friction early] --> B[Direct 1:1 conversation<br/>curious, specific, kind]
    B --> C{Resolved?}
    C -->|Yes| D[Document agreement<br/>+ follow up]
    C -->|No| E[Bring in mentor / project lead<br/>as facilitator]
    E --> F{Resolved?}
    F -->|Yes| D
    F -->|No| G[Escalate to PI<br/>for mediation]
    G --> H[If needed: institutional<br/>processes / HR / ombuds]







Start direct and small. Most friction resolves in a respectful one-on-one. Lead with curiosity (“Help me understand…”) and a specific issue, not an accusation.
Use a facilitator if a direct conversation stalls — a mentor or project lead, not to take sides but to help both people be heard.
Escalate to the PI for mediation when needed.
Use institutional channels (HR, ombuds, Title IX, etc.) for matters of harassment, discrimination, safety, or misconduct — these go beyond the group and must follow institutional policy. The PI helps you access them.







NoteCommunication techniques that help




Observe, then state need. Describe the observable behavior and its impact, then the request — without judgment language. (“When the analysis arrives the night before the meeting, I can’t review it in time; could we set an internal deadline two days earlier?”)
Reflect back. Briefly restate what you heard before responding, so the other person feels understood. Misunderstandings shrink when people feel heard.
Ask, don’t tell, in tense moments. Calibrated, open questions (“How am I supposed to do that with the current timeline?”) invite problem-solving instead of triggering defensiveness.
crumbs: 18  Conflict Resolution, Feedback, and Accountability

title: 18  Conflict Resolution, Feedback, and Accountability
text:
18.5 Accountability — professional, not punitive
We hold real standards. We meet them through development and documentation, not penalties.
When performance or follow-through falls short:

Early, private conversation. Name the gap specifically; ask what’s getting in the way; listen. Often the cause is unclear expectations, overload, or an unsurfaced obstacle — all fixable.
Clarify expectations and support. Restate what “done” looks like, set a realistic plan, and offer help or resources.
Document. Keep a brief, factual record of the conversation, the plan, and the timeline. Documentation protects both parties and keeps accountability fair.
Follow up. Check progress against the plan; recognize improvement.
Use institutional/contractual processes only where applicable and only after the developmental steps — handled through the proper institution or entity, never invented in this manual.







ImportantWhat we explicitly retired



The 2021 manual tied wage status and pay reductions to task completion and precision thresholds (e.g., 50% wage reduction for a missed cleanup step; waged↔︎non-waged conversions). We have removed all punitive wage mechanics. Compensation and employment terms are governed by the relevant institution or entity. Accountability here is about clarity, support, documentation, and the “no-surprises” deadline culture (?sec-communication) — not financial penalty.
crumbs: 18  Conflict Resolution, Feedback, and Accountability

title: 18  Conflict Resolution, Feedback, and Accountability
section: 18.6 The no-surprises principle, applied to accountability
text:
18.6 The no-surprises principle, applied to accountability
Accountability and feedback should never blindside anyone. If something is off, the person hears it from a teammate or mentor early and directly — not for the first time in a review, and never as a penalty out of nowhere. Both directions: leaders surface concerns early, and members surface obstacles early. Surprises are the failure mode we design against.

title: 19  Funding, Grants, Travel, and Professional Development
text:
19.1 How the group is funded
{#sec-funding}
This chapter covers how the group is funded, how members engage with grants, how we support conference travel, and how we invest in each member’s growth — including protecting against burnout.
Funding comes from the PI’s grants and the group’s portfolio of extramural, foundation, society, industry, and institutional support, pursued along the IAP trajectory (seed and trainee support now, building toward R-level and center-scale awards). In keeping with our transparency value, members can learn from our funding work:
crumbs: 19  Funding, Grants, Travel, and Professional Development

title: 19  Funding, Grants, Travel, and Professional Development
text:
Grants are open intra-group. Members may read grant documents (funded or not) in the shared drive — both to learn how grants are written and to see the group’s vision for the years ahead.
You will often be asked to contribute a figure, preliminary analysis, or feedback to a grant. This is real training and a credited contribution.
Purchases or grant charges go through the PI; never commit group funds without approval.


19.1.1 Which entity holds the funds
Funding determines process: the entity that holds an award sets eligibility, spending rules, and reimbursement path (Section 2.2).

Lynn-administered awards and accounts follow Lynn University procurement, travel, and reimbursement procedures; EBDL members use these for Lynn-funded work.
RIPLRT / LLC funds (foundation, society, industry, or consulting awards held by the LLC) follow LLC and sponsor terms.
UPR or external members may also have home-institution funding and travel paths; confirm which applies before incurring costs.

Practical rule: confirm the funding source and its umbrella before you book travel or commit a purchase. Reimbursement runs through the entity that holds the money, and mixing them creates problems that are hard to unwind. When unsure, ask the PI or the named project lead first.
crumbs: 19  Funding, Grants, Travel, and Professional Development

title: 19  Funding, Grants, Travel, and Professional Development
section: 19.2 Engaging with grants as a development activity
text:
19.2 Engaging with grants as a development activity
Grant-writing is part of the development ladder. Depending on your stage, you may:

Build or refine a figure or preliminary-results panel.
Run an analysis that becomes preliminary data.
Draft a biosketch, specific-aims critique, or mentoring-plan section.
Help assemble letters, budgets, or data-management/sharing plans.

Mentees pursuing their own paths are encouraged to apply for fellowships and trainee awards (the group actively supports trainee-support applications, per the IAP). We help you find and write them.
crumbs: 19  Funding, Grants, Travel, and Professional Development

title: 19  Funding, Grants, Travel, and Professional Development
text:
19.3 Travel and conferences
We advocate conference travel to present work, network, and stay current.

Every member presents at least once a year; mentees aim for a regional or (preferably) national conference aligned with their goals.
Cost should not be a barrier. We actively pursue travel awards, scholarships, and trainee grants so members can attend. Some group funds may be available on request.
Plan submissions against the shared abstract calendar (AAAAI, AAI, ATS, SOT, ASM, ISES, ASBMB, ABRCMS, and others).
Confirm authorship before submitting (?sec-authorship), and rehearse as a pod.







NotePlaceholder: travel funding specifics



Exact travel-funding sources, amounts, reimbursement procedures, and institutional travel policies vary and must be confirmed with the PI and the relevant institution for each trip. Apply early for external travel awards regardless.
crumbs: 19  Funding, Grants, Travel, and Professional Development

title: 19  Funding, Grants, Travel, and Professional Development
text:
19.4 Professional development
We invest in members’ growth beyond project deliverables:

IDP-driven. Development goals live in the Individual Development Plan (?sec-mentoring) and are revisited each semester.
Skills. Coding, statistics/ML, scientific writing, presenting, and science communication are all explicitly developed, not assumed.
Sponsorship. Mentors put members forward for opportunities, awards, and roles (?sec-mentoring).
Pathways. We support transitions into graduate, professional, research, data-science, public-health, and leadership positions — a named IAP goal.
crumbs: 19  Funding, Grants, Travel, and Professional Development

title: 19  Funding, Grants, Travel, and Professional Development
text:
19.5 Wellbeing and sustainable productivity
Productivity is a core value, but so is sustainability. A burned-out scientist is neither healthy nor productive.

Protect rest and boundaries. We do not glorify overwork. Connected, rested teams do better science in fewer hours.
Plan the semester. Use a semester plan and weekly writing/analysis blocks (aligned with the IAP cadence) so work is steady rather than frantic.
Watch for burnout — in yourself and teammates — and raise it early. Naming overload is professionalism, not weakness.
Say no strategically. Not every opportunity advances the through-line. Declining or deferring low-alignment requests protects time for high-value work; the PI and project leads help you triage.
Use available support. Institutional wellbeing resources, counseling, and accommodations exist; using them is encouraged, not stigmatized.







TipAlign effort with priorities



The best protection against overwork is alignment: spend your energy on what advances a SMART goal and the through-line, and let the rest go to the backlog. If you’re overwhelmed, that’s a planning conversation to have early with your mentor — not a failing to hide.

20.1 Onboarding
This chapter defines how members join, grow, and leave the group well. Good onboarding makes people productive and connected quickly; good offboarding protects continuity, relationships, and reputation.
New members complete the New Member Onboarding Checklist (/forms/onboarding-checklist.md). At a high level, the first weeks look like this:

title: 20  Onboarding, Training Milestones, and Offboarding

20.1.1 First 7 days

Read this manual; sign the acknowledgment form (/forms/manual-acknowledgment.md).
Meet your mentor and the PI; understand your project and pod.
Get accounts and access: messaging channel, GitHub org, shared drive, project tool, and any project-specific tools — provisioned at least privilege (?sec-data-governance).
Add a short bio and (optional) photo for the group directory; set up your availability.



20.1.2 Step 0 — Confirm your umbrella
Before the first-7-days checklist, your mentor confirms and records which umbrella you join under (Section 2.2), because it sets your IRB, training, and authorship path:

Lynn University (EBDL): Lynn CITI/IRB, Lynn accounts and resources, Lynn policy.
UPR or other external / independent: your home institution’s CITI/IRB and policies; RIPLRT-direct mentoring and any collaboration/DUA terms.

This is captured on the onboarding checklist and the manual-acknowledgment form (/forms) so your record is unambiguous from day one. Offboarding confirms that data, accounts, and products are returned or transferred to the correct entity for the umbrella you worked under.


20.1.3 First 30 days

Complete required CITI/IRB training; be added to relevant IRB protocols before touching human-subjects data.
Complete tool onboarding: Git/GitHub basics, R or Python setup, reproducible-notebook walkthrough, and the data-governance rules.

Co-create your Individual Development Plan with your mentor.



20.1.4 First 90 days

Independently own a named deliverable (a figure, codebook, literature synthesis, or reproducible notebook).
Present once to the pod or group (a wins-and-roadblocks update counts).
Have a first IDP check-in to calibrate goals and support.

title: 20  Onboarding, Training Milestones, and Offboarding
text:
20.3 Offboarding
People move on — graduation, new positions, end of a term, or a planned transition. We offboard deliberately so nothing is lost and relationships stay strong. Members complete the Offboarding Checklist (/forms/offboarding-checklist.md).

20.3.1 Knowledge & continuity handoff

Transfer ownership of repos, documents, and tasks; ensure successors have access.
Document the state of every active project: where things stand, what’s next, where things live.
Ensure all code is committed and pushed, notebooks render, and data is stored per governance rules.
Update the variable dictionary and project operating manual.



20.3.2 Credit & products

Confirm authorship/contributorship on in-progress and completed products (?sec-authorship). Leaving the group does not erase earned credit; departing members remain authors on work they did.
Agree on how in-progress manuscripts will be completed and who leads them.



20.3.3 Access & security

Revoke access appropriately (accounts, repos, drives, data environments) — security hygiene, not distrust.
Return or properly handle any equipment or restricted materials.



20.3.4 Relationship & growth

Final IDP review and a forward-looking conversation: references, recommendation letters, sponsorship, and staying in the network.
Capture the member in the group’s alumni record; alumni remain part of the RIPLRT community and a source of mentorship for current members.
An exit stop/start/continue conversation: what should the group keep, start, or stop? Departing members often give the most candid, useful feedback.







TipOffboarding is a relationship, not a transaction



How we say goodbye shapes our reputation and network as much as how we say hello. Alumni who left well become collaborators, references, recruiters of future members, and ambassadors for the group. Invest in the exit.

text:
21.2 Quarterly: lab climate pulse
A 10-minute anonymous pulse turns belonging into data. It covers: workload, role clarity, sense of belonging, mentorship quality, confidence with tasks, and barriers. The PI and leads review results, share back what they heard, and name one or two concrete changes. Measuring climate without acting on it erodes trust faster than not measuring at all.
crumbs: 21  Annual Review and Manual Maintenance

title: 21  Annual Review and Manual Maintenance
text:
21.3 Annually: the RIPLRT operating review
Once a year we step back and review the group as a whole.

21.3.1 1. Stop / Start / Continue (lab feedback)
Everyone contributes (use /templates/stop-start-continue.qmd): What should the group stop doing? start doing? continue doing? Synthesize themes; commit to a short, public list of changes.


21.3.2 2. Project portfolio review
For each project: Is it advancing? Is it aligned with the through-line and a SMART goal? Is it appropriately staffed? Should it continue, pivot, pause, or close? This prevents drift and overextension — our main risk is too many half-supported projects, not too few people.


21.3.3 3. Authorship audit
Review every active and recent product against the documented contributorship agreements (?sec-authorship): Is credit accurate and fair? Are mentees getting the authorship their contributions earned? Are first-author/co-first-author trainee goals on track? Resolve any drift now, not at submission.


21.3.4 4. Strategic alignment review
Check the portfolio and the group’s activities against the IAP’s 12/36/60-month goals: Are we on pace? What needs to change? Update the goals based on funding, data access, and partner feedback. Refresh the through-line narrative if the science has progressed.


21.3.5 5. Climate and inclusion review
Review the year’s climate pulses for trends. Is the group living its values? Is it inclusive in practice, not just branding? What will we change?
crumbs: 21  Annual Review and Manual Maintenance

title: 21  Annual Review and Manual Maintenance
text:
21.4 Manual maintenance
This manual is itself reviewed annually (and amended as needed in between).
Maintenance process:

Designate a maintainer each year (often the Group Lead, with PI sign-off) to shepherd updates.
Collect proposed changes throughout the year via GitHub issues/PRs (CONTRIBUTING.md) and the annual stop/start/continue.
Review and merge approved changes; update CHANGELOG.md.
Re-render the Quarto book and publish the new version.
Re-acknowledge: when changes are substantive, members re-sign the acknowledgment so everyone is on the current version.







NoteSections to review every year




Tooling and platforms (?sec-project-management) — tools change.
Data governance and dataset rules (?sec-data-governance) — DUAs and IRB terms change.
Responsible AI (?sec-responsible-ai) — this field moves fast.
Institutional placeholders — confirm affiliations, IRB-of-record, and policies.
Vision/Mission/Values and SMART alignment (?sec-authorship and Ch. 4) — keep them synced with the current IAP.
crumbs: 21  Annual Review and Manual Maintenance

title: 21  Annual Review and Manual Maintenance
text:
21.5 Closing the loop
The point of all this review is not bureaucracy — it’s adaptation. We observe how the group is doing (scientifically and humanly), we get feedback, and we change. Self-awareness, feedback, and the willingness to adjust are leadership responsibilities. A group that reviews itself honestly and acts on what it finds is a group that keeps getting better at both the science and the mentoring.
